item.title: Are People With ADHD Symptoms More Likely to Be Left-Handed?
item.description:
ADHD

Are People With ADHD Symptoms More Likely to Be Left-Handed?

A new study investigated hyperactivity/inattention in handedness groups.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • A meta-analysis found that people with ADHD are more likely to be left-handed or mixed-handed.
  • A new study investigated data from almost 8,000 children on handedness and inattention and hyperactivity.
  • Left-handed and mixed-handed children showed more inattention and hyperactivity.

Occasionally, there are anecdotal reports on the internet that people with ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) are more commonly left-handed or mixed-handed than the average person, but is there actually scientific evidence for this idea?

Turns out: there is scientific evidence supporting this idea. In 2022, a meta-analysis on handedness in people with ADHD was published (Nastou et al., 2022). A meta-analysis is a statistical integration of data from several original studies so that the sample size is very large and the results are very trustworthy. The meta-analysis showed that people with ADHD had a statistically significant increase in non-right-handedness (left-handedness and mixed-handedness combined) compared to people without ADHD. People with ADHD had a 27.3% chance of being mixed- or left-handed compared to 18.1% of people without ADHD.

What, however, was unclear in this meta-analysis, was whether attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms (like hyperactivity and inattention symptoms) in people without a clear ADHD diagnosis are also linked to more left-handedness and mixed-handedness.

A new study on the association between handedness and mental health symptoms in children in the general population

A new study entitled “Writing hand preference and child mental health in the general population: Findings from the Millennium Cohort Study,” now published in the scientific journal Laterality, was focused on the association between handedness and mental health symptoms in children in the general population (Sifaki and Flouri, 2026). In the study, conducted by scientists Maria Sifaki and Eirini Flouri from University College London, data from almost 8,000 children (roughly half of them girls) from the U.K.’s Millennium Cohort Study were analyzed.

In this study, the parents of the children reported on several different symptoms their children showed at ages 3, 5, 7, 11, and 14 years. These symptoms included:

  • Emotional difficulties.
  • Conduct difficulties.
  • Hyperactivity/inattention problems.
  • Peer difficulties.
  • Difficulties with prosocial behavior.

Moreover, the children’s handedness was assessed at age 14.

Results of the study: The strongest association was found for hyperactivity/inattention problems

Overall, about 87% of children in the study were right-handed, and about 13% were not right-handed, with about 12% being left-handed and 1% being mixed-handed. The associations with the assessed symptoms were quite interesting.

  • For most symptoms, there were no statistically significant associations at all.
  • For conduct problems, the non-right-handed group had more difficulties than the right-handed group, but only at age 5, not at any other age, showing that the association is not very stable over time.
  • The strongest effects were clearly found for hyperactivity/inattention problems. Here, the non-right-handed group had more difficulties than the right-handed group at ages 5, 7, 11, and 14. Thus, these differences were present at almost all age groups, showing a stable association between hyperactivity/inattention problems and not being right-handed.

Takeaway

The results of the study confirm the results of the earlier meta-analysis, but also broaden them. They show that the association between ADHD and non-right-handedness is not limited to people with a clinical ADHD diagnosis. Instead, also children in the general population with hyperactivity or inattention problems have a higher chance of being left-handed or mixed-handed than children without those symptoms. These findings provide further evidence for a link between neurodiversity and left-handedness and mixed-handedness.

item.title: 'Snacks' That Go Way Beyond Food
item.description:
Creativity

'Snacks' That Go Way Beyond Food

To improve your writing (and maybe your life), consider a new type of "snack."

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • "Snack" time for writing: use micro-chunks instead of rigid routines to maintain momentum.
  • Scheduled mini-naps can be a disciplined, essential reset like regular exercise.
  • Short, inspiring interactions with peers can provide lasting creative energy boosts.

I recently had a Zoom chat with two writing friends—all of us have been nonfiction writers for work for years but we’re trying to become fiction writers. We admitted that we’re stuck right now, for so many reasons. Summer doldrums? Out of the normal routine? Scared to start a big revision? Yes, all of these.

After talking through what is helping (or not), I came away with the idea that I need more snacks, but not food. Let me explain.

Writing Snacks

In the chaos of summer (vacation, kids’ changing schedules, unexpected travel), we discovered our regular writing routines have been fighting to stay on schedule. Each of us felt we’re losing the battle. Carefully carved out time chunks that worked during the regular part of the year don’t work in summer. As we talked it through, we realized those routines need to give way to smaller, less well-planned micro-chunks of time. "Snacks." Instead of three hours three days a week, I may only have an hour, twice a week. Or even less: a few minutes each day or every other day. The time chunks may be smaller, but they need to be there. One of the women has given herself the task of writing a small essay every Friday morning. She writes thoughtful comments on Substack, about 200-250 words, and that anchors her writing. Brilliant. And those essays get done, every week, even if the novel is still percolating.

Nap Snacks

My buddies told me about a woman they had talked with at a writing retreat who is a “dedicated napper.” She takes 20-minute naps on a daily basis. My friends commented that they didn’t have the discipline to do that. The woman, knowing that these two women are dedicated athletes (one is a big mountain biker and the other runs races) said, “You’d never forego your exercise and athletic discipline, right? It’s the same thing with naps. I need them and so I build in a discipline to take them, every day.”

Matisse, illustrating a nap snack
Source: N.K.Napier

As a napper-in-training, I love this idea. Another experiment for August: a nap snack to refresh mind and body, every day. My dog, Matisse, offers a good role model.

Inspiration Snacks

The two women join Zoom weekly and write together. They were kind enough to invite me to the chat as well. We are each writing books that are way outside of our normal nonfiction writing, so we are definitely new at this. We spent 15 minutes talking about (OK, I guess the right word would be “commiserating”) how we’re doing on our projects, what’s helping (books we’re reading, new resources, ideas), and how we’ll move forward. In that short chat, I came away with more energy than I’ve felt in a long time. I needed the inspiration that they offered and hope I did the same for them. Even though it was far too early in the morning for me, I jumped from my chair when we finished and raced to get more coffee so I could get to work.

article continues after advertisement
Inspiration snacks in book form
Source: N.K.Napier

My friend just posted her weekly essay on Substack (Noticing | Kristi Spence | Substack). Her writing snack has given me an inspiration snack for the day.

Now I need to take a nap snack.

item.title: How Hollywood's Teen Movies Get Adolescence Wrong
item.description:
Adolescence

How Hollywood's Teen Movies Get Adolescence Wrong

Why teen films often distort love—plus five that get it right.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Per Bandura's social cognitive theory, teens adopt beliefs and behaviors from characters they admire.
  • A study in the Journal of Children and Media found films often cast actors in their 20s as teens.
  • Research shows 81% of teen movies portray love at first sight and soulmates as literal fact.

Movies and TV that show teen characters who are socially or physically appealing can be very influential on teen audiences, especially if they identify with them. According to Albert Bandura’s social cognitive theory, teens adopt behaviors, beliefs, and self-efficacy through observing others. Unfortunately, many Hollywood films and television have not always done a great job of reflecting teen reality. Many times, they just perpetuate more stereotypes and unrealistic, overly idealized narratives about life and love.

According to a recent study in the Journal of Children and Media, most coming-of-age movies are out of touch with teen reality. Hollywood prefers teen films to be idealized, unrealistic portrayals that overlook their actual identity development. For instance, many films cast actors over 22 years old to play high school students. I have been guilty of doing this myself in the movie The Honor List, where we cast Arden Cho to play a 17-year-old when she was 32 years old. It really does adolescents a disservice to portray them as if all physical signs of puberty are pretty much gone, and they are fully mature adults.

Teen romances are also guilty of unrealistic portrayals of teens’ experience at navigating relationships. Teen romances show idealized love and intimacy without the complexity of how love really is. Some studies have found teens learn romantic beliefs and behaviors from watching romantic movies, which endorse overly romantic ideals. One example is the movie Regretting You (2025), which has two 16-to 17-year-olds managing their feelings of love with ease—as if they were 45 years old. About 81% of teen movies portray “love at first sight” and “soulmates” as fact rather than fiction. If teens assume love is either meant to be or not (or destiny), this can add to the belief that the second conflict arises, it must be time to abandon ship.

5 Films That Get It Right

Here are five movies that have some real teen developmental arcs, issues, and authentic storylines and characters.

Lady Birdy
Source: A24

Lady Bird (2017): This movie entertains and captures real teen issues of social class, anxiety, family troubles, and leaving home with ease. Lady Bird's struggles do not come across as forced but as serious, grounded in her growth into adulthood.

Call Me By Your Name
Source: Sony Pictures Classic
Superbad
Source: Columbia Pictures

Call Me By Your Name (2017): This coming-of-age movie shows first heartbreak in a down-to-earth, realistic way. The message that it is OK to sit with grief is evolved and rare for a coming-of-age movie.

Superbad (2007): This comedy nails the anxiety that underlies much of teen life. The characters are awkward and insecure, as many teens are in real life, as they navigate friendship and rejection in a hilarious way.

Boyhood
Source: Universal Pictures

Boyhood (2014): This epic coming-of-age drama defies most Hollywood films by shooting over 12 years with the same actors aging in real time. Richard Linklater, the director, captures identity development in a true-to-life portrayal of the physical and emotional changes experienced by a child named Mason.

Juno
Source: Fox Searchlight Pictures

Juno (2007): This portrayal of teen pregnancy is not romanticized, but instead awkward and ambivalent. This coming-of-age comedy uses humor to help Juno come to terms with the serious teen issue of pregnancy, which never comes across as moralistic. Juno is just navigating growing up along with all the real mistakes we make along the way.
